useCases.title: Reject invalid numeric values
useCases.scenario: A model stores measurements, rates, or prices that must be ordinary numeric values.

useCases.title: Validate API input
useCases.scenario: An API accepts floating-point input but must not store NaN or infinity.

interview.question: What does FiniteFloat validate?
interview.answer: FiniteFloat validates a value as a float and disallows non-finite values. This means NaN, positive infinity, and negative infinity are rejected.
interview.followUp: How can you apply the same rule without the alias? Use float with AllowInfNan(False) metadata.

interview.question: When should you use FiniteFloat?
interview.answer: A model field annotated with FiniteFloat accepts an ordinary finite number. It raises a validation error for NaN or either infinity.
interview.followUp: What related aliases describe other float ranges? PositiveFloat, NegativeFloat, NonPositiveFloat, and NonNegativeFloat impose sign-based limits.

interview.question: How does FiniteFloat relate to AllowInfNan?
interview.answer: FiniteFloat is a convenience alias supplied by Pydantic. The documentation also describes AllowInfNan as another way to control whether non-finite float values are allowed.
interview.followUp: What does strict mode change? It limits valid inputs to float values and objects with __float__() or __index__().

keyPoints: FiniteFloat requires a finite float value.
AllowInfNan can provide the underlying non-finite-value control.
PositiveFloat is a related alias for values above zero.
NegativeFloat is a related alias for values below zero.
gotchas: FiniteFloat rejects NaN and both positive and negative infinity.

frozen.summary: Set frozen=True to make a Pydantic model faux-immutable and generate a __hash__() method. Hashing is only possible when all attribute values are hashable.
frozen.explanation: The frozen configuration option makes a model faux-immutable: existing attributes cannot be reassigned, and Pydantic generates a __hash__() method. The resulting instance is hashable only when all its attribute values are hashable.

parameters.name: frozen
parameters.description: Whether a model is faux-immutable and whether Pydantic generates its hash method.

frozen.returns: A boolean configuration value controlling model mutability and hash-method generation.

example.title: A faux-immutable model
example.explanation: Setting frozen=True prevents attribute assignment after initialization and causes Pydantic to generate a hash method. Hashing succeeds here because the model's only field contains a hashable string.

useCases.title: Read-only model state
useCases.scenario: Prevent accidental reassignment of validated model attributes in configuration or value-object models.

useCases.title: Hashable value objects
useCases.scenario: Use models as dictionary keys or set members when every field value is hashable.

useCases.title: Functional-style updates
useCases.scenario: Signal that updates should produce a new model instance instead of mutating the current one.

interview.question: What does frozen=True do?
interview.answer: Set model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True) on the model. Pydantic then disallows attribute assignment and generates a __hash__() method.
interview.followUp: Does frozen guarantee hashability? No: hashability still depends on all model attributes being hashable.

interview.question: Is a frozen model deeply immutable?
interview.answer: The model becomes faux-immutable, meaning attempts to assign to its attributes are rejected after construction. The option also requests generation of a hash method.
interview.followUp: What happens if a field contains a list? The model may not be hashable because the list is unhashable, even though assignment to the field is blocked.

interview.question: What is the default value of frozen?
interview.answer: The documented default is False, so ordinary models allow attribute assignment unless frozen is enabled. The setting is the inverse of the older V1 allow_mutation option.
interview.followUp: What was the V1 counterpart? allow_mutation was the inverse setting and defaulted to True.

keyPoints: With frozen=True, assignments to model attributes are prevented after the instance has been created.
Pydantic generates a __hash__() method when frozen is enabled.
A frozen instance can be used as a hashable value only when all its attributes are hashable.
The option is disabled by default, so models are mutable unless configured otherwise.
In Pydantic V1, the corresponding configuration used the inverse name allow_mutation.
gotchas: A frozen model is not guaranteed to be hashable; every attribute value must itself be hashable.
frozen controls attribute assignment rather than providing deep immutability for mutable values stored inside the model.

FutureDate.summary: PastDate is a Pydantic type for dates that must be in the past. It parses supported date inputs and rejects dates that are not earlier than the current date.
FutureDate.explanation: PastDate is a Pydantic type for dates that must be earlier than the current date when validation runs. It adds a past-date rule to normal date validation, so supported date inputs are parsed and then checked against today.
FutureDate.returns: A validated datetime.date value that is in the past.

example.title: Validate a past date
example.explanation: The model accepts a date string in the past and rejects a future date.

useCases.title: Past-only dates
useCases.scenario: Validate a birth date or registration date that cannot be in the future.

useCases.title: Declarative validation
useCases.scenario: Keep date rules in a model field annotation instead of writing a custom validator.

useCases.title: Parse external input
useCases.scenario: Accept date strings while exposing a datetime.date value in Python code.

interview.question: What does PastDate validate?
interview.answer: PastDate is a Pydantic date type with an extra rule: the value must be in the past. It still uses the normal date validation rules for supported inputs.
interview.followUp: How would you require a future date instead? Use FutureDate, which applies the corresponding future-date constraint.

interview.question: Which inputs can become a date?
interview.answer: A date instance is validated as a date. Strings can use the RFC 3339 date format, and numeric values can be Unix timestamps in seconds or milliseconds.
interview.followUp: What happens to a datetime input? It may be accepted as a date only when its time is zero and it has no timezone information.

interview.question: How is PastDate used in a model?
interview.answer: Use PastDate as the field annotation in a Pydantic model. Pydantic parses the input and raises a validation error when the result is not in the past.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the failure? Catch ValidationError and inspect its errors, or use model validation APIs that return structured errors.

keyPoints: PastDate accepts date values only when they are earlier than the current date.
The underlying standard-library type is datetime.date.
Existing date objects are checked directly instead of being converted from text.
Text and byte inputs support the documented date formats and timestamp forms.
When serialized as JSON, date values are written as strings.
Pydantic supplies related constrained date and datetime types for common time rules.
gotchas: The check uses the date at validation time, so a value that passes today may fail later.
Date strings should use the documented RFC 3339 date format.
Numeric inputs can represent seconds or milliseconds since the Unix epoch, depending on configuration.

FutureDatetime.summary: FutureDatetime is a Pydantic type for datetime values that must be in the future when validation runs. A past or current value fails validation.
FutureDatetime.explanation: FutureDatetime is a Pydantic type for datetime values that must be in the future when validation runs. Use it as a model field to reject past datetimes.
FutureDatetime.returns: A validated datetime value that is in the future.

example.title: Require a future datetime
example.explanation: The model accepts a datetime only when it is later than the validation time.

useCases.scenario: An event must start after the model is created.

useCases.title: Check future deadlines
useCases.scenario: A task deadline must not already have passed.

useCases.title: Validate request data
useCases.scenario: An API field must contain a future point in time.

interview.question: What does FutureDatetime validate?
interview.answer: FutureDatetime is a Pydantic type that requires a datetime to be later than the time of validation. A past value raises a validation error.
interview.followUp: What error type is used for a past value? The documentation shows the error type as `datetime_future`.

interview.question: How do you use FutureDatetime in a model?
interview.answer: Use it as a field annotation in a Pydantic model, such as `starts_at: FutureDatetime`. Pydantic then applies the future-time check during model validation.
interview.followUp: How can the check be combined with another datetime rule? Use an annotated datetime with `Field` constraints, as supported by the standard-library datetime types.

interview.question: What input forms can datetime validation accept?
interview.answer: In strict mode, Pydantic accepts only datetime instances for datetime fields. In JSON mode, datetime input can be an RFC 3339 string or a Unix timestamp.
interview.followUp: What happens if a FutureDatetime value is not in the future? Validation fails with the `datetime_future` error type.

keyPoints: FutureDatetime represents a datetime later than the validation time.
Pydantic reports an error when the value is not future-dated.
JSON validation accepts an RFC 3339 datetime string or a Unix timestamp.
Strict mode requires an actual `datetime` object.
gotchas: A value that is now or earlier fails validation.
Strict mode does not accept converted datetime input such as a string.

HttpUrl.summary: HttpUrl validates HTTP and HTTPS URLs. It requires a host and top-level domain, and limits the URL to 2083 characters.
HttpUrl.explanation: HttpUrl validates URLs that use http or https. It requires a host and a top-level domain, limits the URL length to 2083 characters, and exposes parsed parts such as scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment.
HttpUrl.returns: A validated Pydantic URL object with parsed URL properties.

example.title: Validate an HTTP URL
example.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, HttpUrl

class Site(BaseModel):
    url: HttpUrl

site = Site(url="https://example.com/docs")
print(site.url)
print(site.url.host)
print(site.url.path)
example.explanation: The model converts the input string into an HttpUrl and exposes URL parts such as the host and path.

interview.question: What does HttpUrl validate?
interview.answer: HttpUrl accepts only http and https URLs. It requires a host and a top-level domain, and it has a maximum length of 2083 characters.
interview.followUp: How can a model require a database name in a PostgresDsn? Add a field validator and check that the parsed path exists and has more than one character.

interview.question: Which URL parts can code access?
interview.answer: After validation, the value is a URL object rather than just the original string. Its scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment can be read as properties.
interview.followUp: What would you inspect to enforce an application-specific rule? Use a field validator and inspect the parsed URL properties.

interview.question: How are international domains handled?
interview.answer: Pydantic converts international host names and top-level domains to punycode. This gives the stored URL an ASCII host representation.
interview.followUp: What other host-name behavior should you check? Pydantic allows underscores in domain parts except the top-level domain.

keyPoints: Use HttpUrl when the URL must use HTTP or HTTPS, include a host and TLD, and stay within 2083 characters.
AnyUrl accepts any scheme and does not require a top-level domain, but it still requires a host.
AnyHttpUrl restricts the scheme to HTTP or HTTPS while allowing a host without a top-level domain.
FileUrl validates file URLs and does not require a host.
PostgresDsn requires user information and a host, and it can represent multiple hosts.
The parsed scheme is always available; other URL components are available when present.
gotchas: Non-ASCII host names and top-level domains are converted to punycode.
Underscores can be accepted in domain parts other than the top-level domain, even though this may not match hostname rules.

ImportString.summary: ImportString lets a Pydantic field load a Python object from an import path. It accepts paths using dot or colon syntax and can also accept the object directly.
ImportString.explanation: ImportString converts an importable Python path into the referenced Python object during model validation. The path can use a dot or a colon between a module and its attribute, and an already imported object can also be provided.
ImportString.returns: The imported Python object represented by the input path.

example.title: Import a function from a dotted path
example.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ImportString

class Settings(BaseModel):
    function: ImportString

settings = Settings(function='math.cos')
assert settings.function(0) == 1
print(settings.model_dump_json())
example.explanation: The string is imported when the model is created, so the field contains the Python function.

useCases.scenario: Load a configured function by name without hard-coding the function in the model.

useCases.title: Importable plugins
useCases.scenario: Store a Python class or callable as a validated model field.

useCases.title: Serializable object references
useCases.scenario: Write an import path to JSON while using the resolved object in Python.

interview.question: What does ImportString do?
interview.answer: ImportString is a Pydantic type that accepts an importable Python path and resolves it to the referenced object during model creation. The path may use either module.attribute or module:attribute syntax.
interview.followUp: What happens if the path cannot be imported? Validation fails with an import error.

interview.question: What values can an ImportString field accept?
interview.answer: A field can receive the object itself, such as math.cos, or a string such as 'math.cos'. Both forms produce the same imported object after validation.
interview.followUp: Can a string be used as a default? Yes, but default validation must be enabled.

interview.question: How is an ImportString value serialized?
interview.answer: ImportString values can be serialized to JSON. The serialized value is the import path for the object, such as 'math.cos'.
interview.followUp: What path form is preferred when a module and attribute name could conflict with a submodule? The documentation says a dot path prefers the module.

keyPoints: It resolves an importable Python path to the referenced Python object.
Use either a dot or a colon between the module and its attribute.
Resolution happens when the model instance is created.
You may pass the Python object directly instead of passing a path string.
An ImportString field can be included in JSON output as an import path.
gotchas: A string default is not evaluated unless the field enables default validation, for example with validate_default=True.

interview.question: What does InstanceOf do in Pydantic?
interview.answer: InstanceOf is a generic annotation that checks whether the input is an instance of the specified class. For example, InstanceOf[Plugin] accepts Plugin objects and rejects values that fail the isinstance check.
interview.followUp: What error occurs for a rejected value? The validation error uses the is_instance_of error type and reports the expected class.

interview.question: How do you declare an InstanceOf field?
interview.answer: Use it as a field annotation, such as plugin: InstanceOf[Plugin]. Pydantic then validates the field with an instance check rather than normal structural validation.
interview.followUp: Can it accept a subclass? Yes. A subclass is also an instance of its parent class under Python's isinstance rules.

interview.question: What happens when validation fails?
interview.answer: A value that is not an instance of the required class fails validation. The error identifies the field and includes the expected class name.
interview.followUp: How would you allow several classes? Use a union of InstanceOf annotations, such as InstanceOf[A] | InstanceOf[B].

keyPoints: Use InstanceOf[ClassName] when a field must contain an object of a particular class.
Validation succeeds only when Python's isinstance check returns True.
For JSON input, Pydantic validates the value as the wrapped type.
A failed check reports that the input should be an instance of the required class.

interview.question: What is the difference between an implicit and a named type alias?
interview.answer: An implicit alias is a type expression assigned to a variable, such as an Annotated integer. A named alias is declared with the type statement or TypeAliasType, so Pydantic can preserve its name in JSON Schema definitions.
interview.followUp: When should you prefer a named alias? Prefer it when the alias is reused in a model schema or when it is recursive, because Pydantic can emit a shared definition and resolve recursion.

interview.question: How do you create a reusable constrained type?
interview.answer: Use Annotated to combine a base type with validation metadata. For example, Annotated[int, Field(gt=0)] accepts only positive integers when validated by Pydantic.
interview.followUp: Can the constraint be independent of Pydantic? Yes. Constraints from annotated-types, such as Gt(0), can make the alias usable without importing Pydantic for the constraint itself.

interview.question: How do you define a recursive JSON type alias?
interview.answer: A recursive alias must have a name that Pydantic can resolve while building its schema. TypeAliasType can hold a quoted recursive expression, such as a JSON value made from dictionaries, lists, scalar values, and None.
interview.followUp: Why is the recursive expression quoted in the TypeAliasType form? The alias is evaluated before its name exists, so the quote delays evaluation until Pydantic resolves the definition.

keyPoints: Use Annotated to define a validation rule once and reuse it in several fields.
Named aliases let Pydantic retain the alias name instead of treating the assigned variable as anonymous.
A named alias can produce one JSON Schema definition and references to it when multiple fields use the alias.
Use a named alias for recursive structures such as nested JSON values.
Aliases can be generic, so one reusable constrained container can work with different item types.
gotchas: Do not put field-specific metadata, such as a field default, inside a reusable type alias.
For a recursive alias defined with TypeAliasType, write the recursive expression as a string.

interview.answer: model_post_init is an instance method that performs additional initialization after the model is created. Pydantic calls it after __init__ and model_construct, when the model's fields are available.

interview.question: What is the signature of model_post_init?

interview.question: When should you use model_post_init instead of a custom __init__?
interview.answer: Use a model_post_init implementation when an operation needs the whole model. Field or model validators are alternatives when the work belongs to validation itself.
interview.followUp: Why avoid a custom __init__ for this? The documentation says custom initialization can lose validation settings such as strictness, extra-data behavior, and context.

interview.question: What is the difference between plain and wrap model serializers?
interview.answer: `model_serializer` customizes serialization for the whole model. Plain mode is called directly and supplies the output; wrap mode receives a handler that delegates to Pydantic's normal serialization.
interview.followUp: When would you choose wrap mode? Use it when you need to keep or extend Pydantic's normal output, such as adding a derived entry.

interview.question: What function signatures can a model serializer use?
interview.answer: The decorator supports plain serializer functions with `(self)` or `(self, info)`. Wrap functions use `(self, nxt)` or `(self, nxt, info)`, where `nxt` is the serialization handler.
interview.followUp: What should a wrap serializer do if it needs the default output? Call `nxt(self)` and then modify the returned value.

interview.question: How does Pydantic use a serializer return type?
interview.answer: A serializer's return type can be declared with a return annotation or the decorator's `return_type` argument. Pydantic uses that type to build an extra serializer and check the serialized value against it.
interview.followUp: What happens if the serializer returns a string instead of a dictionary? `model_dump()` can return that string, although normal type checking expects a dictionary unless the method type is overridden for type checkers.

interview.question: How do Pydantic models handle input types?
interview.answer: Pydantic models declare fields with Python type annotations. During validation, Pydantic checks the input and can convert compatible values, such as a numeric string to an integer, unless stricter behavior is configured.
interview.followUp: What is the risk of this conversion? A conversion can discard information, so strict validation may be better when exact input types matter.

You can set the output type and choose when the function runs. With when_used='json', normal Python dumps keep the integer, while JSON output uses the formatted string.

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function that changes the serialized value.

parameters.name: return_type
parameters.description: Type produced by the serializer. If omitted, Pydantic infers it from the function annotation.

parameters.name: when_used
parameters.description: When the serializer is active: always, unless-none, json, or json-unless-none.

PlainSerializer.returns: A serialized value produced by the function; its declared type can be controlled with return_type.

example.title: Format an integer for JSON
example.code:
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic.functional_serializers import PlainSerializer

CommaInt = Annotated[int, PlainSerializer(lambda value: f'{value:,}', return_type=str, when_used='json')]

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    total: CommaInt

invoice = Invoice(total=1234)
print(invoice.model_dump())
print(invoice.model_dump_json())
example.explanation: The serializer changes the integer to a formatted string only when the model is serialized as JSON.

useCases.title: Reusable annotated serialization
useCases.scenario: You need one reusable formatting rule for a type used by several model fields.

useCases.title: JSON-only formatting
useCases.scenario: You want JSON output to use a different representation while Python-mode dumps keep the original value.

interview.question: What does PlainSerializer do?
interview.answer: PlainSerializer is used with an annotated type to change its serialized output. Its function runs instead of the normal serialization logic for that value.
interview.followUp: When would a wrap serializer be better? Use it when the custom code should receive a handler and optionally call the standard serialization logic before changing the result.

interview.question: What is return_type used for?
interview.answer: return_type declares the type produced by the serializer. If it is omitted, Pydantic infers it from the function's return annotation.
interview.followUp: What happens if the returned value has the wrong type? Pydantic does not validate the serialized value against the original field type, so the serializer should return the intended type.

interview.question: How can PlainSerializer run only for JSON output?
interview.answer: when_used controls when the serializer runs. Its documented values are always, unless-none, json, and json-unless-none; the default is always.
interview.followUp: How can JSON-only formatting be implemented? Set when_used='json', so Python-mode serialization keeps the normal value while JSON-mode serialization uses the custom function.

keyPoints: PlainSerializer changes the serialized form by calling the function you provide.
Attach it to an Annotated type when the same serialization rule should travel with that type.
Use return_type to declare the serializer's output type, or let Pydantic infer it from the annotation.
when_used selects the serialization modes in which the function is active.
The related field_serializer decorator can target every field with '*', but PlainSerializer itself is attached to an annotated type.
gotchas: A plain serializer replaces the normal serialization logic for the field. It does not call Pydantic's standard serializer.
Only one serializer can be defined for a field or model. You cannot stack plain and wrap serializers on the same target.
The serializer's result is not checked against the annotated field type. Return the type you intend to produce.

interview.question: What does PlainValidator do?
interview.answer: PlainValidator runs in place of the field's normal validation. Its returned value becomes the field value, even when that value does not match the annotated type.
interview.followUp: How can JSON Schema describe accepted inputs? Set json_schema_input_type on PlainValidator to the input type or union of input types.

interview.question: How is PlainValidator different from a before validator?
interview.answer: It receives the raw field value and returns a value. Unlike a before validator, it stops further validation, so Pydantic does not validate the result against the field type.
interview.followUp: When should it be avoided? Avoid it when the field must still receive Pydantic's normal type checks.

interview.question: How can you define a plain validator?
interview.answer: Use the Annotated pattern with PlainValidator, or use field_validator with mode='plain'. The function should contain the conversion or checking logic and return the final value.
interview.followUp: What happens if the function returns the input unchanged? That value is accepted, even if it fails the annotated type's normal validation.

populate_by_name.summary: Enables aliased fields to accept input by their Python attribute names as well as their aliases. It defaults to false and is not recommended from Pydantic v2.11 onward because it will be deprecated in v3.
populate_by_name.explanation: When enabled, an aliased field accepts input under both its Python attribute name and its configured alias. The setting defaults to false, and current documentation advises replacing it with validate_by_name together with validate_by_alias because populate_by_name is deprecated for Pydantic v3.

parameters.description: Whether aliased fields may also be populated using their model attribute names.

example.title: Populate an aliased field by name
example.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True)
    my_field: str = Field(alias='my_alias')

print(Model(my_field='value'))
print(Model(my_alias='value'))
example.explanation: Both the field name and its alias can be used when creating the model.

interview.question: What does populate_by_name do?
interview.answer: It allows an aliased field to be populated using either the model attribute name or its alias. The default is false, so only the configured behavior is available unless the setting is enabled.
interview.followUp: What should replace it in newer Pydantic code? Use validate_by_name=True and validate_by_alias=True in ConfigDict.

interview.question: What is its default behavior?
interview.answer: The setting defaults to false. With it enabled, a field declared with an alias can receive input using its Python name as well as that alias.
interview.followUp: Why might enabling both validation options be necessary? It preserves acceptance of both naming forms while avoiding the deprecated setting.

interview.question: Is populate_by_name still recommended?
interview.answer: The current documentation says its use is not recommended from v2.11 onward and that it will be deprecated in v3. The recommended replacement is separate validation controls for names and aliases.
interview.followUp: Can both replacement options be disabled? No; the documentation states that disabling both would make it impossible to populate an attribute.

When enabled, the alias remains accepted alongside the attribute name.
If not configured, the setting is disabled.

PositiveFloat.summary: PositiveFloat is a Pydantic type alias for a float greater than zero. It rejects zero and negative values during validation.
PositiveFloat.explanation: PositiveFloat is a Pydantic type alias for a float with a strict greater-than-zero constraint. Use it as a model field when zero and negative values are invalid.
PositiveFloat.returns: A validated float greater than zero.

interview.question: What does PositiveFloat validate?
interview.answer: PositiveFloat validates a float value and requires it to be greater than zero. A value such as 1.0 is valid, while -1.0 is rejected.
interview.followUp: How would you allow zero too? Use NonNegativeFloat, which requires the value to be greater than or equal to zero.

interview.question: When should you use PositiveFloat?
interview.answer: It is useful for fields such as prices, quantities, or durations when the value must be above zero. Pydantic raises a validation error when the constraint fails.
interview.followUp: What error constraint is reported for a value below the limit? The error type is greater_than, with a greater-than limit of 0.

interview.question: How is PositiveFloat defined?
interview.answer: PositiveFloat is equivalent to an annotated float with a greater-than constraint of 0. This makes the rule explicit in the field type.
interview.followUp: How could you express the same rule directly? Use Annotated[float, Gt(0)] with the appropriate annotated-types metadata.

The alias uses an annotated float and a greater-than constraint.

gotchas: Zero is invalid because the constraint is strictly greater than zero.

interview.answer: PositiveInt is a Pydantic type alias for an integer constrained with a greater-than-zero rule. A field using it accepts positive integers and rejects values that are zero or negative.
interview.followUp: How would you allow zero? Use NonNegativeInt, which applies a greater-than-or-equal-to-zero constraint.

interview.question: How do you use PositiveInt in a model?

interview.question: Which boundary values are accepted?
interview.answer: PositiveInt uses a strict lower bound of zero. Therefore, 1 is valid, while 0 and -1 fail validation.
interview.followUp: What type expresses the opposite boundary? NegativeInt requires a value less than zero.

PrivateAttr.summary: PrivateAttr declares internal model attributes that Pydantic does not validate or serialize normally. Give it a default value or a factory to create the value.
PrivateAttr.explanation: PrivateAttr declares an attribute for internal model state. Pydantic does not validate it or include it in normal model serialization. Its value can come from a default or a factory.
PrivateAttr.syntax:
PrivateAttr(default=..., *, init=False)
PrivateAttr(*, default_factory=..., init=False)
PrivateAttr(*, init=False)

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: The initial value for the private attribute. The default is PydanticUndefined.

parameters.name: default_factory
parameters.type: Callable[[], Any] | Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Any] | None
parameters.description: A callable that creates the value. It may take no arguments or one dictionary containing validated data and initialized private attributes.

parameters.name: init
parameters.description: Whether to include the attribute in a dataclass constructor. This is always False.

PrivateAttr.returns: An instance of ModelPrivateAttr, exposed through the declared private attribute.

example.title: Private model attribute
example.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, PrivateAttr

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    _token: str = PrivateAttr(default="hidden")

user = User(name="Ada")
print(user.name)
print(user._token)
print(user.model_dump())
example.explanation: The private value is available on the object, but it is not part of normal validation or serialized model data.

interview.question: When should PrivateAttr be used?
interview.answer: Use PrivateAttr when a model needs internal state that should not be treated as input data. The attribute is not handled by normal validation or serialization.
interview.followUp: How can the state be initialized? Set a default, or use default_factory to create it when the model instance is created.

interview.question: How can a private attribute get its initial value?
interview.answer: PrivateAttr accepts a default value, a default_factory, or neither. A factory creates the value when needed and may take validated model data as its argument.
interview.followUp: What happens if both options are supplied? Pydantic raises a TypeError.

interview.question: How does Pydantic distinguish private attributes from fields?
interview.answer: Private attribute names start with an underscore and are stored in the model's private-attribute collection. They are not model fields and are not included in the model schema.
interview.followUp: Are dunder names supported? No. Names such as __attr__ are ignored by the model definition.

A factory can take no arguments or receive validated model data and initialized private attributes.
Pydantic records the model's private attributes in __private_attributes__.

Do not provide both a default value and a default factory.

interview.question: What is PydanticCustomError used for?
interview.answer: PydanticCustomError lets a validator define a custom error type, message template, and context. It is raised from the validator when the input fails a rule.
interview.followUp: How are dynamic values added to the message? Pass a context dictionary whose keys match placeholders in the message template.

interview.question: What are its constructor arguments?
interview.answer: The first argument is the error type, the second is the message template, and the optional third argument supplies values for template placeholders. The type is typically a stable snake_case string.
interview.followUp: What happens if the template needs a value that is missing from context? Formatting cannot supply that placeholder, so the context must contain every required key.

interview.question: How does the formatted message work?
interview.answer: The message() method returns the template after its context variables have been inserted. The context and template are also available as attributes.

PydanticUseDefault.summary: PydanticUseDefault is an exception that custom validators can raise to make Pydantic use a field's default value. It is useful when a special input, such as None, should select that default.
PydanticUseDefault.explanation: PydanticUseDefault is an exception from pydantic_core that custom validation code can raise when validation should use the field's default value instead. It can redirect validation away from the supplied value.

example.title: Use a field default during validation
example.code:
from typing import Annotated, Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, BeforeValidator
from pydantic_core import PydanticUseDefault

def use_default_for_none(value: Any) -> Any:
    if value is None:
        raise PydanticUseDefault()
    return value

class User(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[str, BeforeValidator(use_default_for_none)] = "Anonymous"

print(User(name=None))
# name='Anonymous'
example.explanation: The validator raises PydanticUseDefault when the input is None, so Pydantic uses the field's declared default.

useCases.title: Skip standard validation

interview.question: What does PydanticUseDefault do?
interview.answer: Raise PydanticUseDefault from a custom validator when the field should take its declared default instead of continuing with the supplied input. For example, a before validator can raise it when the input is None.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from returning the default? Raising the exception tells Pydantic to follow its default-value validation path, rather than treating the returned value as ordinary validator output.

interview.question: Where is PydanticUseDefault defined?
interview.answer: It is imported from pydantic_core and can be raised by a custom validation function. Pydantic then uses the field's standard default value.
interview.followUp: What happens if the field has no default? The exception cannot provide a value itself, so the model does not gain a replacement value from it.

interview.question: How is it used inside a validator?
interview.answer: A validator can inspect the input and raise PydanticUseDefault for a special case, such as None or an invalid presence value. If it does not raise the exception, normal validation continues with the returned value.
interview.followUp: Why might a before validator be useful here? It can detect the special raw input before later type validation runs.

keyPoints: It tells Pydantic to stop or bypass standard validation for the current value.
The field's declared default becomes the replacement value.
Raising it changes validation control flow instead of returning a normal field value.
Import the exception from pydantic_core.
Use it inside custom validators when a special input should select the default.
gotchas: Raise it only when the field has a suitable default; otherwise there is no useful replacement value.
PydanticUseDefault is for custom validation functions, not for ordinary application errors or serialization failures.

print(credentials.password)                  # **********
print(credentials.model_dump_json())         # masked JSON

interview.question: What does SerializeAsAny do?
interview.answer: SerializeAsAny is an annotation that changes how a field is serialized. The field is validated as its wrapped type, but its actual value is serialized as if the annotation were Any.
interview.followUp: What happens to static type checking? It treats SerializeAsAny[T] like T, so the annotation does not change the type checker view.

interview.question: How does it affect subclass serialization?

interview.followUp: How can the same behavior be enabled for one call? Pass serialize_as_any=True to a serialization method such as model_dump().

interview.question: When should field-level and runtime settings be used?
interview.answer: Use SerializeAsAny[T] in the field declaration when the behavior should always apply to that field. Use serialize_as_any=True when duck-typed serialization is needed for a particular serialization call.

interview.question: What does strict mode change?
interview.answer: Strict mode makes Pydantic less willing to convert input values. For example, lax validation can turn "123" into 123, while strict validation rejects that string for an integer field.
interview.followUp: How can strictness be limited to one field? Use Field(strict=True) or Annotated[int, Strict()] on that field.

interview.question: How do you enable strict mode for one validation call?
interview.answer: You can pass strict=True to model_validate() or a TypeAdapter validation method. This applies strict validation for that validation call.
interview.followUp: Does this affect every later validation call? No. Call-level strictness applies only to the current validation operation.

interview.question: Where can strictness be configured?
interview.answer: Strictness can be configured on a field with Field(strict=True), on a model with ConfigDict(strict=True), or through Strict metadata. A field can override model-level strictness with Field(strict=False).
interview.followUp: What happens when model strictness is enabled but a field sets strict=False? That field uses lax validation and may coerce compatible input.

keyPoints: Lax mode tries to convert compatible values to the target type.
Strict mode reduces coercion and reports an error when the input is not the expected type.
You can enable it for a validation call, a field, or the model configuration.
The Annotated pattern lets you add Strict() directly to a type annotation.
StrictBool, StrictInt, StrictFloat, StrictStr, and StrictBytes are ready-made strict type aliases.
gotchas: Turning on strict mode can break callers that relied on automatic conversion, such as converting a string to an integer.
Strict validation may still accept some JSON representations. For example, a JSON date string can validate as a date.

StrictBool.summary: StrictBool accepts only real boolean values. It prevents the coercion that a regular bool field allows for inputs such as 0, 1, or selected strings.
StrictBool.explanation: StrictBool accepts only boolean values, unlike the regular bool type, which also converts certain integers, strings, and bytes. Use StrictBool when input coercion would be unsafe or unwanted.

example.title: Strict boolean and constrained string
example.code:
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints, StrictBool

class Settings(BaseModel):
    enabled: StrictBool
    code: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(to_upper=True, pattern=r"[A-Z0-9]{3}-[A-Z0-9]{3}")]

settings = Settings(enabled=True, code="abc-123")
print(settings)
example.explanation: The boolean must already be a real bool. The string is converted to uppercase and must match the pattern.

useCases.title: Strict configuration input
useCases.scenario: Configuration flags must reject values supplied as strings or numbers.

useCases.title: Type-safe input validation
useCases.scenario: An API or data pipeline must preserve the original boolean type.

interview.question: What does StrictBool change compared with bool?
interview.answer: StrictBool validates only boolean values. It does not coerce integers, strings, or bytes into booleans.
interview.followUp: What does a regular bool field accept? It accepts True or False, 0 or 1, selected strings such as 'true' and 'no', and bytes that decode to those strings.

interview.question: When should StrictBool be used?
interview.answer: Use StrictBool when the input must already have boolean type. This prevents accidental acceptance of values such as 1, 'yes', or 'false'.
interview.followUp: How can strictness be applied without using a named strict type? Use the Strict() metadata class.

interview.question: How is StrictBool related to Strict()?
interview.answer: Pydantic provides StrictBool as a convenience for applying Strict() metadata to a boolean field. Both approaches enforce strict boolean validation.
interview.followUp: What other strict types are available? Pydantic documents StrictBytes, StrictFloat, StrictInt, and StrictStr.

keyPoints: StrictBool is one of Pydantic's built-in strict types.
StrictBool requires a value with boolean type instead of converting another type.
You can choose the named StrictBool type or use Strict() metadata.
Strict validation allows only actual boolean values.
gotchas: StrictBool is separate from StrictInt behavior: Python treats bool as an int subtype, but strict integer validation still rejects bool.
Strict types reject compatible values that would normally be converted. For StrictBool, the input must be a boolean value.

StrictInt.summary: StrictInt makes Pydantic require an integer instead of converting compatible values. It rejects bool and accepts other integer subtypes.
StrictInt.explanation: StrictInt validates only integer values and rejects bool, even though bool is an int subclass in Python. It is useful when conversion from compatible input types would hide invalid data.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value being checked must be an integer and is not coerced from compatible types.

example.title: Require an integer without coercion
example.explanation: The integer value passes. The float value fails instead of being converted to an integer.

useCases.title: Validate integer fields

interview.question: What does StrictInt do?
interview.answer: StrictInt enables strict validation for an integer field. It accepts an integer value but rejects values such as a float that might otherwise be converted.
interview.followUp: Does it accept bool? No. StrictInt explicitly rejects bool even though Python treats bool as a subclass of int.

interview.question: Which strict scalar types does Pydantic provide?
interview.answer: Pydantic provides StrictBool, StrictBytes, StrictFloat, StrictInt, and StrictStr. These types require the validated value to have the matching type or a permitted subtype.
interview.followUp: What exception applies to StrictFloat? It rejects int input, so an integer is not accepted as a strict float.

interview.question: How can strict validation be combined with other constraints?
interview.answer: Constrained types expose the same behavior with their strict field. This lets a field combine strictness with rules such as bounds, length, or collection constraints.
interview.followUp: How can string constraints be expressed with better type-checker compatibility? Use Annotated with StringConstraints instead of constr.

A strict type accepts its own type or a subtype, subject to documented exceptions.
Constrained types can enable strict behavior through their strict field.
FiniteFloat rejects infinity, negative infinity, and NaN.
gotchas: StrictInt rejects bool values, despite bool being a subclass of int in Python.
StrictFloat does not accept integer input.
StrictBytes accepts both bytes and bytearray.

StrictStr.explanation: Strict types make validation reject compatible values that would normally be converted. `StrictStr`, `StrictInt`, `StrictFloat`, `StrictBool`, and `StrictBytes` require the matching type, with documented subtype rules and exceptions.

interview.question: What problem do Pydantic strict types solve?
interview.answer: Strict types prevent coercion from compatible types. Pydantic provides `StrictBool`, `StrictBytes`, `StrictFloat`, `StrictInt`, and `StrictStr`; validation requires the corresponding type, subject to documented subtype rules.
interview.followUp: How can strictness be combined with other rules? Use the `strict` option on a constrained type such as `conint`, `confloat`, or `constr`, then add its supported constraints.

interview.question: What are the important numeric exceptions?
interview.answer: `StrictInt` accepts integer values but rejects `bool`. This exception exists even though `bool` is an `int` subclass in Python. Other integer subclasses can work.
interview.followUp: What happens with `StrictFloat`? Integer input is rejected, unlike ordinary non-strict numeric validation.

interview.question: When should `FiniteFloat` be used?
interview.answer: `FiniteFloat` accepts only finite floating-point values. It rejects positive infinity, negative infinity, and NaN, so it can be used when those values are invalid.
interview.followUp: Can string constraints be used without `constr`? Yes. `StringConstraints` can be placed in `Annotated`, which also gives type checkers better compatibility.

The available strict aliases cover Boolean, bytes, float, integer, and string values.
A strict value may be an instance of the required type or one of its subtypes, except where a documented caveat applies.
Constrained types can enable the same behavior through their `strict` field.
`FiniteFloat` is available when infinity and NaN must be rejected.

Tag.summary: An alias gives a Pydantic field another name for input and output data. Use it when external data names differ from Python attribute names.
Tag.explanation: An alias gives a Pydantic field another name for input and output data. Use it when the data format and Python naming style use different names.

parameters.name: alias
parameters.description: The external field name used as the alias. It must be a string.

Tag.returns: A field configured with an alternative name for input and output data.

example.title: Use a field alias
example.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class User(BaseModel):
    user_name: str = Field(alias='userName')

user = User.model_validate({'userName': 'Ada'})
print(user.user_name)
print(user.model_dump(by_alias=True))
example.explanation: The model accepts the external name userName and stores the value in the Python field user_name. Serialization uses the alias when by_alias=True is selected.

useCases.title: Map API names
useCases.scenario: An API sends camelCase keys while Python code uses snake_case attributes.

useCases.title: Match an external schema
useCases.scenario: A database or file format requires fixed field names.

useCases.title: Separate internal and external names
useCases.scenario: A model needs to expose Python-friendly names internally and wire-format names externally.

interview.question: What is a Pydantic field alias?
interview.answer: An alias is another name for a model field. It lets Pydantic map an external data name to the Python attribute name during validation and serialization.
interview.followUp: How can serialization use the alias? Call model_dump(by_alias=True) to emit the alias instead of the Python field name.

interview.question: How do you define and use an alias?
interview.answer: Set alias on Field, and pass the external name when validating input. The model still exposes the declared Python attribute name.
interview.followUp: What happens when the input uses the Python name instead? That depends on the model's validation configuration; configure validation by field name if that input must also work.

interview.question: When should aliases be used?
interview.answer: Aliases are useful when an API, database, or file format uses names that do not match Python conventions. They keep the external format separate from the model's internal attribute names.
interview.followUp: How would you emit external names only when needed? Keep normal dumps by field name and pass by_alias=True at the serialization boundary.

keyPoints: Define a field alias with the alias argument on Field.
The alias value must be a string.
The Python attribute keeps its declared name while the alias represents the external name.
Aliases support both loading data and writing serialized data.
gotchas: An alias affects both reading input data and writing serialized data, so choose the external name carefully.

TypeAdapter.summary: TypeAdapter lets you validate, serialize, and generate JSON Schema for a Python type without creating a BaseModel. It works with types such as collections, dataclasses, primitive types, and TypedDicts.
TypeAdapter.explanation: Create a TypeAdapter for a Python type when you need Pydantic validation, serialization, or JSON Schema without defining a BaseModel. The adapter uses the type to build a core schema, then provides methods such as validate_python, validate_json, dump_python, dump_json, and json_schema.
TypeAdapter.syntax:
TypeAdapter(type, config=None)
adapter.validate_python(object)
adapter.validate_json(data)
adapter.dump_python(instance)
adapter.dump_json(instance)
adapter.json_schema()

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: The Python type associated with the adapter.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Optional configuration for the adapter, supplied as a ConfigDict.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: Python object to validate.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: JSON input to validate.

parameters.name: __instance
parameters.description: Value to serialize as JSON.

TypeAdapter.returns: Validation methods return the adapted type T. dump_json returns bytes. rebuild returns None when rebuilding is unnecessary, or True/False when rebuilding was attempted. json_schemas returns a tuple containing per-adapter schemas and shared definitions.

example.title: Validate and serialize a list
example.code:
from typing_extensions import TypedDict
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

class User(TypedDict):
    name: str
    id: int

adapter = TypeAdapter(list[User])
users = adapter.validate_python([{"name": "Fred", "id": "3"}])
print(users)
print(adapter.dump_json(users))
example.explanation: This validates a list of typed dictionaries, converts the string ID to an integer, and serializes the result as JSON bytes.

interview.question: What problem does TypeAdapter solve?
interview.answer: TypeAdapter applies Pydantic validation and serialization to arbitrary supported Python types. This includes primitive types, dataclasses, TypedDicts, and collections such as list[Model].
interview.followUp: How would you reduce repeated validation overhead? Create the TypeAdapter once and reuse it, because schema creation has non-trivial overhead.

interview.question: How do the main validation methods differ?
interview.answer: validate_python checks a Python object against the adapted type and returns the validated value. validate_json does the same for JSON text, bytes, or bytearray.
interview.followUp: When would validate_json be useful? Use it when input is JSON from an external source, because validation can report shape changes in that source.

interview.question: What output operations does TypeAdapter provide?
interview.answer: dump_json serializes an adapted value to JSON and returns bytes. dump_python returns a Python representation, and json_schema generates a JSON Schema for the adapted type.
interview.followUp: What is a key difference from BaseModel.model_dump_json? BaseModel.model_dump_json returns a string for compatibility, while TypeAdapter.dump_json returns bytes.

keyPoints: TypeAdapter performs validation and serialization based on a Python type.
It supports these operations without requiring a BaseModel.
Its methods provide some BaseModel-like functionality for types that do not have those methods.
It can parse data into types that Pydantic supports as model fields.
TypeAdapter.json_schemas can create one JSON Schema result with definitions shared by multiple adapters.
rebuild attempts to create the core schema again, which helps when forward references were unresolved.
gotchas: Do not use a TypeAdapter instance as a field annotation. Use the adapted Python type in annotations instead.
dump_json returns bytes rather than a string. Decode the result if code requires text.
Creating an adapter builds a schema and has overhead. Reuse one adapter in loops or other performance-sensitive code.
When adapting a Pydantic dataclass, validate_python does not support from_attributes.

TypeAdapter.json_schema.summary: `TypeAdapter.json_schema()` returns a JSON Schema dictionary for an adapted type. It supports aliases, reference templates, union formats, custom schema generators, and validation or serialization mode.
TypeAdapter.json_schema.explanation: Call `json_schema()` on a `TypeAdapter` to get a JSON Schema dictionary for its adapted type. The method can choose aliases, reference formats, union output, a schema generator, and validation or serialization mode.
TypeAdapter.json_schema.syntax: TypeAdapter.json_schema(*, by_alias=None, ref_template=DEFAULT_REF_TEMPLATE, union_format='any_of', schema_generator=GenerateJsonSchema, mode='validation')

parameters.name: by_alias
parameters.description: Use aliases as schema keys, or use field names when false. If omitted, configuration decides.

parameters.name: ref_template
parameters.description: Format for references to definitions.

parameters.name: union_format
parameters.description: Union format: `any_of` or `primitive_type_array`.

parameters.name: schema_generator
parameters.description: Schema generator class used to create the schema.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Schema mode: `validation` or `serialization`.

TypeAdapter.json_schema.returns: A dictionary containing the JSON schema for the adapted type.

example.title: Create a schema for a typed list
example.code:
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

adapter = TypeAdapter(list[int])

print(adapter.json_schema())
# {'items': {'type': 'integer'}, 'type': 'array'}
example.explanation: This creates a schema for a list of integers.

interview.question: What does TypeAdapter.json_schema() return?
interview.answer: `TypeAdapter.json_schema()` returns a JSON-compatible dictionary that describes the adapted type. For example, an adapter for `list[int]` produces an array schema whose items are integers.
interview.followUp: How can you describe serialized output instead? Pass `mode='serialization'`; this can differ from the validation schema, such as for types serialized as strings.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the by_alias parameter?
interview.answer: `by_alias` controls whether field aliases are used as property names. If it is `None`, the adapter configuration decides; an explicit Boolean takes precedence.
interview.followUp: How would you change reference names without changing property aliases? Pass a different `ref_template`, such as `#/components/schemas/{model}`.

interview.question: How does union_format affect the generated schema?
interview.answer: The `union_format` argument controls how union schemas are combined. `any_of` is the default, while `primitive_type_array` can use a type array when every branch is a simple primitive without extra constraints or metadata.
interview.followUp: What happens when the primitive type array form cannot represent the union? Pydantic falls back to `anyOf`.

keyPoints: The method builds a schema for the type held by the adapter, including arbitrary types such as `list[int]`.
The result is a dictionary, so it can be inspected directly or passed to JSON encoding.
Use `union_format` to select the representation used for union branches.
The `mode` parameter selects either `validation` or `serialization` schema generation.
Pass a `GenerateJsonSchema` subclass through `schema_generator` to customize schema generation logic.
gotchas: `json_schema()` returns a schema dictionary. It does not serialize a value to a JSON string.
The default mode describes validation. Use `mode='serialization'` when the schema should describe serialized output.

interview.question: What problem does TypeAdapter solve?
interview.answer: TypeAdapter validates and serializes arbitrary Pydantic-compatible types without creating a BaseModel. It is useful for lists, primitive types, dataclasses, and other types that do not provide model methods.
interview.followUp: How would you validate JSON directly? Use validate_json with a string or bytes value, instead of decoding it first.

interview.question: What does validate_python do?
interview.answer: validate_python checks a Python object against the adapted type and returns the converted value when validation succeeds. It accepts strict, from_attributes, and context options.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to from_attributes? It is not supported for Pydantic dataclasses used with TypeAdapter.

interview.question: Can TypeAdapter validate collections?
interview.answer: TypeAdapter can be used with a generic type such as list[User]. It validates each item and reports errors using the path to the invalid value.
interview.followUp: What does validate_json accept? It accepts JSON as either str or bytes and can also receive strict and context options.

You can validate a type directly, so a wrapper model is not required.
The adapted type can be any type that Pydantic supports in model fields.
validate_json checks JSON supplied as text or bytes.
validate_strings validates objects whose input data is represented by strings.
get_default_value returns the wrapped type's default when one is defined.
gotchas: Do not use TypeAdapter itself as the annotation for a BaseModel field. Use the underlying type as the annotation instead.

use_enum_values.summary: `use_enum_values=True` makes Pydantic populate enum fields with their underlying values rather than enum members. Optional enum defaults need `validate_default=True` for this conversion to apply.
use_enum_values.explanation: Set `use_enum_values=True` in `ConfigDict` to make validated enum fields hold their underlying values instead of enum members. For an optional enum default, add `validate_default=True` to its `Field`, because conversion happens during validation.
use_enum_values.returns: The setting changes populated field values; the documented example shows `model_dump()` containing underlying enum values.

example.title: Store enum values
example.code:
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class Flavor(Enum):
    VANILLA = "vanilla"
    CHOCOLATE = "chocolate"

class Order(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(use_enum_values=True)
    flavor: Flavor
    fallback: Optional[Flavor] = Field(
        default=Flavor.VANILLA, validate_default=True
    )

order = Order(flavor=Flavor.CHOCOLATE)
assert order.model_dump() == {"flavor": "chocolate", "fallback": "vanilla"}
print(order.model_dump())
example.explanation: The model stores enum values and validates the optional default so it is converted as well.

useCases.title: Value-oriented output
useCases.scenario: Models whose dumped data is sent to JSON APIs or persistence layers.

useCases.title: Consistent defaults
useCases.scenario: Schemas containing optional enum fields with defaults.

useCases.title: Simpler downstream processing
useCases.scenario: Applications that compare or transform dumped data using primitive values.

interview.question: How do you configure a Pydantic model to use enum values?
interview.answer: Set `model_config = ConfigDict(use_enum_values=True)` on the model. Enum inputs are then populated using each enum member's `value`, which is also convenient when calling `model_dump()`.
interview.followUp: Why might an optional enum default remain an enum member? Because defaults are not validated automatically in this case; enable `validate_default=True` on the field.

interview.question: What is the default behavior of `use_enum_values`?
interview.answer: The setting defaults to `False`, so the model otherwise retains raw enum members. With it enabled, a member such as `SomeEnum.BAR` is represented by its underlying value, such as `'bar'`.
interview.followUp: Where does the conversion occur? During validation, rather than during serialization, which explains the need to validate relevant defaults.

interview.question: How should optional enum defaults be handled?
interview.answer: Add `Field(default=..., validate_default=True)` to an optional enum field that has a default. This causes the default to pass through validation and receive the same value extraction as supplied input.
interview.followUp: What output should be expected from `model_dump()` after enabling the option? Enum fields appear as their underlying values, including validated defaults.

keyPoints: When enabled, enum-typed fields are populated with each member's underlying `value` instead of the enum object.
The option is useful when a later `model_dump()` should contain serialization-friendly enum values.
The setting is disabled by default; enable it explicitly in the model configuration.
Enum value extraction happens during validation, not when the model is serialized.
The documented example shows `model_dump()` returning strings such as `'bar'` and `'foo'` after the option is enabled.
gotchas: An optional enum field with a default needs `validate_default=True`; otherwise its default is not converted.

UUID1.summary: UUID1 is a Pydantic type for a UUID version 1. Use it as a model field annotation to require that UUID version.
UUID1.explanation: UUID1 is a Pydantic type for fields that must contain a valid version 1 UUID. It can be used as a model field annotation, and Pydantic validates the supplied value when creating the model.
UUID1.returns: A validated uuid.UUID value with version 1.

example.title: Validate a version 1 UUID
example.code:
from uuid import UUID
from pydantic import BaseModel, UUID1

class Model(BaseModel):
    request_id: UUID1

model = Model(request_id=UUID('6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8'))
print(model.request_id.version)  # 1
example.explanation: This model accepts only a valid version 1 UUID.

useCases.title: Validate request identifiers
useCases.scenario: An API field must contain a UUID version 1.

useCases.title: Enforce identifier format
useCases.scenario: A model stores identifiers with a fixed UUID version.

useCases.title: Declare a precise field type
useCases.scenario: A schema should describe a version-specific UUID.

interview.question: What does UUID1 validate?
interview.answer: UUID1 is a Pydantic type that requires a valid UUID of version 1. Use it as the annotation for a model field.
interview.followUp: How would you require another UUID version? Use the matching Pydantic type, such as UUID4 or UUID7, when that type is available.

interview.question: How do you use UUID1 in a model?
interview.answer: Define the field with UUID1 in a Pydantic BaseModel. Pydantic then validates the input during model creation.
interview.followUp: What happens if the input has another UUID version? Validation fails because UUID1 requires version 1.

interview.question: How is UUID1 defined?
interview.answer: UUID1 is a constrained UUID type. Its underlying declaration is an Annotated UUID with UuidVersion(1).
interview.followUp: Why use a constrained type instead of plain UUID? It expresses the required UUID version in the field type.

keyPoints: UUID1 accepts only UUID values whose version is 1.
The type is based on uuid.UUID plus Pydantic metadata that requires version 1.
Import UUID1 and BaseModel when declaring a model field with this type.

    ...

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class User(BaseModel, validate_assignment=True):
    name: str
    age: int

user = User(name="Ada", age=36)
user.age = "37"
assert user.age == 37

try:
    user.age = "not an integer"
except ValidationError:
    print("assignment rejected")
example.explanation: The first assignment is converted to an integer; the second raises a validation error.

interview.question: What does `validate_assignment` change?
interview.answer: By default, Pydantic validates data when the model is created, but not when an attribute is changed. Enabling `validate_assignment` makes later assignments undergo validation too.
interview.followUp: How can it be enabled? Use `validate_assignment=True` as a model class keyword argument or set it in `model_config`.

interview.question: How do you enable assignment validation?
interview.answer: It can be enabled directly in the class definition with `class User(BaseModel, validate_assignment=True)`. This causes assignments such as `user.age = ...` to be validated after construction.
interview.followUp: What happens without the setting? An invalid value can be assigned without revalidation.

interview.question: What is the default behavior?
interview.answer: The setting is a configuration option whose default is `False`. With the default, validation occurs only during model creation; with it enabled, validation also occurs when model data changes.
interview.followUp: Why might this matter? It preserves the model’s validation guarantees across its full mutable lifetime.

interview.question: What does validate_call do?
interview.answer: It wraps a function and validates its arguments from the function's annotations before calling the function. It can also validate the return value when validate_return=True.
interview.followUp: What happens to an unannotated parameter? It is treated as Any, so the decorator does not apply a specific type constraint.

interview.question: Does it coerce input values?
interview.answer: The decorator normally coerces compatible inputs. For example, a numeric string can be converted to an integer before the function receives it.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent unwanted conversion? Use a custom configuration with strict validation enabled.

interview.question: Which function signatures can it validate?
interview.answer: It supports positional, keyword-only, positional-only, variable positional, and variable keyword parameters. It also works with async functions.
interview.followUp: How can trusted callers bypass validation? Call the decorated function's raw_function attribute, while accepting the loss of validation.

interview.question: What does ValidateAs do?
interview.answer: ValidateAs is an annotation helper for custom types. It tells Pydantic to validate the input using a supported type, then calls a hook to build the custom type.
interview.followUp: What is the order of operations? Pydantic first validates against from_type, then passes that result to instantiation_hook.

interview.question: How is ValidateAs used in a type annotation?
interview.answer: Use Annotated with ValidateAs and pass both the supported validation type and a conversion callable. A TypeAdapter can then validate the input and return the custom object.
interview.followUp: Can the supported type be a model? Yes. The documented pattern uses a BaseModel as from_type.

interview.question: What is the purpose of instantiation_hook?
interview.answer: The hook takes the validated from_type value and returns the populated custom type. This separates input validation from custom-object construction.

interview.answer: ValidationError reports that input failed Pydantic validation. It can be caught and printed or inspected programmatically; the documentation example shows its string form identifying the model, field, message, error type, and input details.
interview.followUp: How would you handle several invalid fields? Inspect the structured error collection rather than parsing the formatted string, then map each location to an appropriate application response.

interview.question: When can ValidationError be raised by model configuration?
interview.answer: It is raised when a configured validation rule rejects input, such as forbidding an extra field. The resulting diagnostic identifies where validation failed and why.
interview.followUp: What should an API return? Convert the structured diagnostics into your API's error format while avoiding exposure of sensitive input values.

interview.question: What information does a validation error provide?
interview.answer: The displayed diagnostic includes the field location, a validation message, an error type, and information about the received input. This makes the exception useful both for debugging and for building field-level error responses.
interview.followUp: Why prefer structured diagnostics? They remain machine-readable when wording changes and can be grouped by location or error type.

interview.answer: A plain validator can return a value immediately. Pydantic then skips its normal validation for that field, so even a value that does not match the annotation can be accepted.

interview.question: What does WithJsonSchema do?
interview.answer: WithJsonSchema is an Annotated annotation that overrides the schema generated for a type. It is useful for types that do not produce a JSON Schema by default, such as Callable.
interview.followUp: How can the override differ between validation and serialization? Set the mode argument so the annotation applies only to the selected schema generation mode.

interview.question: How do you use WithJsonSchema?

interview.followUp: What changes for a list element? Put the annotation on the element type, and its replacement becomes the schema under the list's items key.

It can describe types for which Pydantic normally cannot create a schema.
The optional mode setting limits the override to one schema generation mode.
The documentation recommends this annotation as the simpler option for custom schema changes.
gotchas: The replacement is complete. If the schema needs a type, add the type inside the WithJsonSchema dictionary.
For fields with validators, use json_schema_input_type instead when you need to describe the accepted input schema.
A mode-specific schema affects only validation or serialization generation, depending on the selected mode.

WrapSerializer.summary: Pydantic functional serializers change serialized output for fields, types, or whole models. Plain serializers replace normal logic; wrap serializers can call normal logic and then modify its result.
WrapSerializer.explanation: Functional serializers let you change how Pydantic serializes fields, types, or whole models. Use a plain serializer to replace normal serialization, or a wrap serializer to call and then modify the normal serializer.
WrapSerializer.syntax:
field_serializer(*fields, mode='plain' | 'wrap', return_type=..., when_used='always', check_fields=...)
model_serializer(mode='plain' | 'wrap', when_used='always', return_type=...)
PlainSerializer(function, return_type=..., when_used='always')
WrapSerializer(function, return_type=..., when_used='always')

parameters.name: *fields
parameters.description: Field names targeted by the decorator.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Serialization mode: 'plain' or 'wrap'.

parameters.name: return_type
parameters.description: Optional output type. If omitted, Pydantic infers it from the annotation.

parameters.name: when_used
parameters.description: When the serializer runs: 'always', 'unless-none', 'json', or 'json-unless-none'.

parameters.name: check_fields
parameters.description: Whether to verify that the named fields exist on the model.

WrapSerializer.returns: The decorators return the decorated serializer function. Serialization produces the function's returned value; a model serializer may return a non-dictionary value.

example.title: A wrap serializer
example.code:
from typing import Annotated, Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, SerializationInfo, WrapSerializer

def utc_serializer(value: Any, handler, info: SerializationInfo):
    serialized = handler(value)
    if info.mode == "json":
        return serialized
    return serialized

UTCValue = Annotated[Any, WrapSerializer(utc_serializer)]

class Event(BaseModel):
    value: UTCValue

print(Event(value="hello").model_dump())
example.explanation: WrapSerializer receives the value and can call the handler to use the normal serialization logic before changing the result.

interview.question: What does field_serializer do?
interview.answer: @field_serializer changes serialization for one or more fields. It supports plain mode, which replaces the normal logic, and wrap mode, which can call the normal serializer through a handler.
interview.followUp: How can one serializer apply to every field? Pass the special field name '*' to @field_serializer.

interview.question: When would you use model_serializer?
interview.answer: @model_serializer customizes the serialized result for the whole model. Its function can return a dictionary or another type, so the result does not always have to be a dictionary.
interview.followUp: What type should a model_dump override use when a model serializer returns a non-dictionary? In an if TYPE_CHECKING block, override model_dump with the actual return type.

interview.question: What is the difference between PlainSerializer and WrapSerializer?
interview.answer: PlainSerializer changes a type's serialized value by calling a simple function. WrapSerializer receives the original value and a handler for the standard serialization, so it can modify the input or the standard result.
interview.followUp: How can a serializer run only for JSON output? Set when_used='json'; normal model_dump output keeps the original Python value.

keyPoints: Use field_serializer for selected fields and model_serializer for the complete model output.
A field serializer may be an instance method or a function, with optional serialization information and a wrap handler.
when_used controls whether a serializer runs always, for non-None values, for JSON, or for JSON non-None values.
PlainSerializer is useful when the normal serialization result can be replaced by one direct function.
WrapSerializer can preprocess the value, call standard serialization, and then change the result.
Use '*' with field_serializer to apply one serializer to every field.
gotchas: Plain mode replaces the default serialization. Wrap mode gives the function a handler, but the function must decide whether to call it.
field_serializer needs at least one field name.
If return_type is not provided, Pydantic infers it from the function annotation.

WrapValidator.summary: Functional validators add custom checks or transformations to Pydantic fields and models. They can be written with Annotated or validator decorators.
WrapValidator.explanation: Functional validators let you add custom checks or transformations to Pydantic fields and models. You can attach them with Annotated metadata or decorator methods.

parameters.name: field

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Controls when the validator runs: 'before', 'after', 'plain', or 'wrap'.

parameters.name: check_fields
parameters.description: Whether to check that the named fields exist on the model.

parameters.name: json_schema_input_type
parameters.description: Input type used only when generating validation-mode JSON Schema for before, plain, or wrap validators.

WrapValidator.returns: A callable decorator for the validator method; the validator itself returns the validated value or model.

interview.question: What is an after field validator?
interview.answer: An after validator runs after Pydantic's normal field validation. It receives the converted value, checks or changes it, and must return the value.
interview.followUp: When would a before validator help? Use it when the raw input needs preprocessing before Pydantic validates its type.

interview.question: What makes a wrap validator different?
interview.answer: A wrap validator receives a handler. It can call that handler to run inner validation, catch its errors, change the input, return a fallback, or stop validation early.
interview.followUp: How can a wrap validator retry validation? Catch a ValidationError, adjust the input, and call the handler again.

interview.question: When should you use a model validator?
interview.answer: A model validator checks the model as a whole. It is useful for rules involving several fields, such as requiring two dimensions to match.
interview.followUp: What does an after model validator return? It returns the validated model instance, commonly using Self as its return type.

keyPoints: A field validator receives a value and returns the validated value.
Field validators have four modes: after, before, plain, and wrap.
After validators receive a value after Pydantic's built-in conversion and checks.
Wrap validators can run code before or after inner validation, or skip it.
Use Annotated metadata for reusable validators or use @field_validator for class-specific field rules.
gotchas: Custom validators do not run for default field values unless validation of defaults is enabled.
With Annotated validators, before and wrap functions run from right to left, while after functions run from left to right.
